claim: The default mode network (DMN) is involved in higher-order cognition including semantic cognition, mental time travel, and scene construction.
source: The default mode network (DMN) is involved in higher-order cognition including in semantic cognition, mental time travel, and scene construction (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010a; Ralph et al., 2017; Spreng et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010a; Ralph et al., 2017; Spreng et al., 2009).

claim: The DMN often deactivates in response to visual inputs.
source: it often deactivates in response to visual inputs yet it is connected to visual cortex (Knapen, 2021; Leech et al., 2012; Szinte and Knapen, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Knapen, 2021; Leech et al., 2012; Szinte and Knapen, 2020).

claim: The DMN is connected to visual cortex.
source: it often deactivates in response to visual inputs yet it is connected to visual cortex (Knapen, 2021; Leech et al., 2012; Szinte and Knapen, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Knapen, 2021; Leech et al., 2012; Szinte and Knapen, 2020).

claim: The DMN is associated with abstraction from sensory-motor features.
source: In addition, this network is associated with both abstraction from sensory-motor features (; Chiou et al., 2019; Gonzalez Alam et al., 2021; Rice et al., 2015b; Rice et al., 2015a) and internally generated states like imagery and autobiographical memory (Philippi et al., 2015; Ritchey and Cooper, 2020; Spreng and Grady, 2010; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Chiou et al., 2019; Gonzalez Alam et al., 2021; Rice et al., 2015b; Rice et al., 2015a).

claim: The DMN is associated with internally generated states like imagery and autobiographical memory.
source: In addition, this network is associated with both abstraction from sensory-motor features (; Chiou et al., 2019; Gonzalez Alam et al., 2021; Rice et al., 2015b; Rice et al., 2015a) and internally generated states like imagery and autobiographical memory (Philippi et al., 2015; Ritchey and Cooper, 2020; Spreng and Grady, 2010; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Philippi et al., 2015; Ritchey and Cooper, 2020; Spreng and Grady, 2010; Zhang et al., 2022).

claim: DMN is maximally separated from sensory-motor regions in terms of physical location and connectivity space.
source: DMN is maximally separated from sensory-motor regions – both in terms of its physical location and in connectivity space.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is based on established scientific knowledge about DMN organization.

claim: DMN is at one end of the principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity that captures the separation of unimodal and heteromodal cortex.
source: It is at one end of the principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity that captures the separation of unimodal and heteromodal cortex (Margulies et al., 2016) and this location is thought to allow DMN to sustain representations that are distinct from sensory-motor features and at odds with the current state of the external world (Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Margulies et al., 2016.

claim: The location of DMN in connectivity space allows it to sustain representations that are distinct from sensory-motor features and at odds with the current state of the external world.
source: It is at one end of the principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity that captures the separation of unimodal and heteromodal cortex (Margulies et al., 2016) and this location is thought to allow DMN to sustain representations that are distinct from sensory-motor features and at odds with the current state of the external world (Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018) and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Parcellations of intrinsic connectivity reveal subdivisions within the DMN.
source: Despite these common functional characteristics of DMN, parcellations of intrinsic connectivity reveal subdivisions (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; Schaefer et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2020; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; Schaefer et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2020; Yeo et al., 2011).

claim: Lateral fronto-temporal (FT) DMN regions are associated with semantic cognition.
source: Lateral fronto-temporal (FT) DMN regions are associated with semantic cognition, including the abstraction of heteromodal meanings from sensory-motor features and the ability to access these meanings from sensory inputs in a task-appropriate way (; Chiou et al., 2019; Ralph et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Chiou et al., 2019; Ralph et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Scene construction is a key component of episodic recollection.
source: In contrast, scene construction, thought to be a key component of episodic recollection, is associated with a medial temporal (MT) subsystem (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; D'Argembeau et al., 2010; Hassabis et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phrase 'thought to be' and citations (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; D'Argembeau et al., 2010; Hassabis et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2022).

claim: Scene construction is associated with a medial temporal (MT) subsystem of the DMN.
source: In contrast, scene construction, thought to be a key component of episodic recollection, is associated with a medial temporal (MT) subsystem (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; D'Argembeau et al., 2010; Hassabis et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010b; D'Argembeau et al., 2010; Hassabis et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2022).

claim: FT and MT-DMN subnetworks are interdigitated in regions of core DMN.
source: FT and MT-DMN subnetworks are interdigitated in regions of core DMN (Braga and Buckner, 2017) and they are assumed to work together but little is known about how information within them is integrated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Braga and Buckner, 2017.

claim: Objects engage a ventral pathway extending laterally and anteriorly through ventral lateral occipital cortex (LOC) and the fusiform gyrus towards the anterior temporal lobes (ATL).
source: Objects engage a ventral pathway extending laterally and anteriorly through ventral lateral occipital cortex (LOC) and the fusiform gyrus towards the anterior temporal lobes (ATL), thought to be a key heteromodal hub for conceptual representation.
evidence: The claim is stated directly and represents established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: The anterior temporal lobes (ATL) are thought to be a key heteromodal hub for conceptual representation.
source: Objects engage a ventral pathway extending laterally and anteriorly through ventral lateral occipital cortex (LOC) and the fusiform gyrus towards the anterior temporal lobes (ATL), thought to be a key heteromodal hub for conceptual representation.
evidence: The claim is indicated by 'thought to be' and represents a theoretical interpretation based on prior research.

claim: The ventral visual pathway might act as input to FT-DMN.
source: This pathway might act as input to FT-DMN (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Andrews-Hanna and Grilli, 2021; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Kravitz et al., 2013; Malach et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is indicated by 'might' and is supported by multiple citations (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Andrews-Hanna and Grilli, 2021; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Kravitz et al., 2013; Malach et al., 2002).

claim: Navigating visuospatial environments and scene construction involves the occipital place area, posterior cingulate, retrosplenial, entorhinal, and parahippocampal cortex, before this pathway terminates in hippocampus.
source: Navigating visuospatial environments and scene construction, on the other hand, involves the occipital place area, posterior cingulate, retrosplenial, entorhinal, and parahippocampal cortex, before this pathway terminates in hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is stated directly and represents established knowledge in spatial cognition research.

claim: Regions involved in navigating visuospatial environments and scene construction are associated with the MT-DMN subnetwork.
source: These regions are associated with the MT-DMN subnetwork (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Andrews-Hanna and Grilli, 2021; Epstein and Baker, 2019; Kravitz et al., 2011; Reagh and Yassa, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Andrews-Hanna and Grilli, 2021; Epstein and Baker, 2019; Kravitz et al., 2011; Reagh and Yassa, 2014).

claim: During memory for people and places, medial parietal cortex mirrors the well-established medial-lateral organisation of ventral temporal cortex during the perception of scenes and faces.
source: For example, during memory for people and places, medial parietal cortex mirrors the well-established medial-lateral organisation of ventral temporal cortex during the perception of scenes and faces; medial parietal regions also show differential connectivity to these visual regions (Margulies et al., 2009; Silson et al., 2019; Steel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Margulies et al., 2009; Silson et al., 2019; Steel et al., 2021).

claim: Medial parietal regions show differential connectivity to visual regions involved in scene and face perception.
source: For example, during memory for people and places, medial parietal cortex mirrors the well-established medial-lateral organisation of ventral temporal cortex during the perception of scenes and faces; medial parietal regions also show differential connectivity to these visual regions (Margulies et al., 2009; Silson et al., 2019; Steel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Margulies et al., 2009; Silson et al., 2019; Steel et al., 2021).

claim: Participants showed poorer accuracy in the spatial context task relative to the semantic task.
source: There was a main effect of task (F(1,26)=76.52, p<0.001), condition (F(1,26)=11.31, p=0.002) and a task by condition interaction (F(1,26)=14.51, p<0.001). Participants showed poorer accuracy in the spatial context task relative to the semantic task and in the MCB relative to the SCB condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (F(1,26)=76.52, p<0.001).

claim: Participants showed poorer accuracy in the MCB relative to the SCB condition.
source: There was a main effect of task (F(1,26)=76.52, p<0.001), condition (F(1,26)=11.31, p=0.002) and a task by condition interaction (F(1,26)=14.51, p<0.001). Participants showed poorer accuracy in the spatial context task relative to the semantic task and in the MCB relative to the SCB condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (F(1,26)=11.31, p=0.002).

claim: Participants were significantly less accurate in the MCB trials relative to the SCB trials of the spatial context task.
source: Participants were significantly less accurate in the MCB trials relative to the SCB trials of the spatial context task (t(26)=4.08, p<0.001); this difference was not observed in the semantic task (t(26)=0.74, p=0.47).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (t(26)=4.08, p<0.001).

claim: The difference in accuracy between MCB and SCB trials was not observed in the semantic task.
source: Participants were significantly less accurate in the MCB trials relative to the SCB trials of the spatial context task (t(26)=4.08, p<0.001); this difference was not observed in the semantic task (t(26)=0.74, p=0.47).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (t(26)=0.74, p=0.47).

claim: Participants had slower reaction times in the spatial context task than the semantic task.
source: Response times showed the same pattern, with main effects of task (F(1,26)=51.37, p<0.001), condition (F(1,26)=31.14, p<0.001), and their interaction (F(1,26)=29.48, p<0.001). Participants had slower reaction times in the spatial context task than the semantic task and in the MCB relative to the SCB condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (F(1,26)=51.37, p<0.001).

claim: Participants had slower reaction times in the MCB relative to the SCB condition.
source: Response times showed the same pattern, with main effects of task (F(1,26)=51.37, p<0.001), condition (F(1,26)=31.14, p<0.001), and their interaction (F(1,26)=29.48, p<0.001). Participants had slower reaction times in the spatial context task than the semantic task and in the MCB relative to the SCB condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (F(1,26)=31.14, p<0.001).

claim: Participants were significantly slower in MCB than SCB trials of the spatial context task.
source: Post hoc comparisons confirmed that participants were significantly slower in MCB than SCB trials of the spatial context task (t(26)=6.08, p<0.001), but this difference was not observed in the semantic task (t(26)=0.1, p=0.92).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (t(26)=6.08, p<0.001).

claim: The difference in reaction times between MCB and SCB trials was not observed in the semantic task.
source: Post hoc comparisons confirmed that participants were significantly slower in MCB than SCB trials of the spatial context task (t(26)=6.08, p<0.001), but this difference was not observed in the semantic task (t(26)=0.1, p=0.92).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Study 1 (t(26)=0.1, p=0.92).

claim: Semantic probes elicited greater activation in bilateral ventral LOC, extending to fusiform cortex and supramarginal gyrus in the left hemisphere.
source: Semantic probes elicited greater activation in bilateral ventral LOC, extending to fusiform cortex and supramarginal gyrus in the left hemisphere.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data from Study 1 showing differential activation patterns.

claim: Spatial context probes elicited a stronger response in bilateral dorsal LOC, medial occipital lobe, precuneus, parahippocampal cortex and supplementary motor areas (SMA).
source: Spatial context probes elicited a stronger response in bilateral dorsal LOC, medial occipital lobe, precuneus, parahippocampal cortex and supplementary motor areas (SMA), as well as insula and middle frontal gyrus and frontal pole regions in the left hemisphere, and precentral regions in the right hemisphere (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data from Study 1 showing differential activation patterns, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Regions engaged by the spatial context probes resembled scene perception regions.
source: Regions engaged by the spatial context probes resembled scene perception regions, while semantic probes overlapped with object perception regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of task activation with localizer data from Study 2, as shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Semantic probes overlapped with object perception regions.
source: Regions engaged by the spatial context probes resembled scene perception regions, while semantic probes overlapped with object perception regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of task activation with localizer data from Study 2, as shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: MT-DMN showed a significantly stronger response to spatial context relative to semantic probes.
source: Post hoc comparisons showed a significantly stronger response within MT-DMN to spatial context relative to semantic probes (t(26)=4.1, p=0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data from Study 1 (t(26)=4.1, p=0.001), as shown in Figure 2d.

claim: No significant difference between tasks was observed for core or FT-DMN during the probe phase.
source: No significant difference between tasks was observed for core or FT-DMN (both p>0.05, Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data from Study 1 (both p>0.05), as shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Visual areas responding to semantic and spatial context probes showed differential connectivity, including to regions of DMN.
source: Visual areas responding to semantic and spatial context probes showed differential connectivity, including to regions of DMN (posterior cingulate, medial prefrontal cortex, portions of anterior and dorsal prefrontal cortex, and anterior temporal cortex; Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic connectivity analysis from Study 3, as shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Semantic probe connectivity was associated with perceptual and somatomotor terms.
source: Cognitive decoding using Neurosynth revealed that semantic probe connectivity was associated with perceptual and somatomotor terms, while spatial context probe connectivity was associated with navigation, visuospatial and episodic memory terms (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by cognitive decoding analysis using Neurosynth, as shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Spatial context probe connectivity was associated with navigation, visuospatial and episodic memory terms.
source: Cognitive decoding using Neurosynth revealed that semantic probe connectivity was associated with perceptual and somatomotor terms, while spatial context probe connectivity was associated with navigation, visuospatial and episodic memory terms (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by cognitive decoding analysis using Neurosynth, as shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Semantic probe regions showed preferential overlap with FT-DMN.
source: Semantic probe regions showed preferential overlap with FT-DMN, whilst spatial context probe regions showed greater overlap with MT-DMN, followed by core DMN (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with Yeo et al., 2011 parcellation, as shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Spatial context probe regions showed greater overlap with MT-DMN, followed by core DMN.
source: Semantic probe regions showed preferential overlap with FT-DMN, whilst spatial context probe regions showed greater overlap with MT-DMN, followed by core DMN (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with Yeo et al., 2011 parcellation, as shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Semantic decisions elicited stronger engagement within dorsolateral prefrontal, lateral occipital, posterior temporal, and occipital cortex, as well as pre-SMA.
source: Figure 3a shows that semantic decisions elicited stronger engagement within dorsolateral prefrontal, lateral occipital, posterior temporal, and occipital cortex, as well as pre-SMA.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data from Study 1, as shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Regions activated by semantic decisions overlapped with FT-DMN.
source: These regions overlapped with FT-DMN (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with Yeo et al., 2011 parcellation, as shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Spatial context decisions produced stronger activation within a predominantly medial set of occipital, ventromedial temporal (including parahippocampal gyrus), retrosplenial, and precuneus regions.
source: Spatial context decisions produced stronger activation within a predominantly medial set of occipital, ventromedial temporal (including parahippocampal gyrus), retrosplenial, and precuneus regions that overlapped with MT-DMN (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data from Study 1, as shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Regions activated by spatial context decisions overlapped with MT-DMN.
source: Spatial context decisions produced stronger activation within a predominantly medial set of occipital, ventromedial temporal (including parahippocampal gyrus), retrosplenial, and precuneus regions that overlapped with MT-DMN (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with Yeo et al., 2011 parcellation, as shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Visual ROI sensitive to scenes showed a stronger response to spatial context decisions relative to semantic decisions.
source: Post hoc comparisons showed a stronger response to spatial context decisions, relative to semantic decisions, in the visual ROI sensitive to scenes (t(26)=3.63, p<0.001), but not in the object-selective region (t(26)=1.88 p=0.071; Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data from Study 1 (t(26)=3.63, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Object-selective visual region did not show a significant difference in response to spatial context versus semantic decisions.
source: Post hoc comparisons showed a stronger response to spatial context decisions, relative to semantic decisions, in the visual ROI sensitive to scenes (t(26)=3.63, p<0.001), but not in the object-selective region (t(26)=1.88 p=0.071; Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data from Study 1 (t(26)=1.88 p=0.071), as shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Semantic decision regions showed stronger connectivity to lateral visual regions along with lateral temporal cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, angular gyrus, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.
source: Semantic decision regions showed stronger connectivity to lateral visual regions along with lateral temporal cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, angular gyrus, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic connectivity analysis from Study 3, as shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Spatial decision regions were more connected to medial visual regions, ventro-medial temporal regions, medial parietal cortex, ventral parts of medial prefrontal cortex, motor cortex and dorsal parts of LOC.
source: Spatial decision regions were more connected to medial visual regions, ventro-medial temporal regions, medial parietal cortex, ventral parts of medial prefrontal cortex, motor cortex and dorsal parts of LOC.
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic connectivity analysis from Study 3, as shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The semantic decision network was associated with terms related to language, semantic processing, and reading.
source: Cognitive decoding of these connectivity maps using Neurosynth (Figure 3f) revealed that the semantic decision network was associated with terms related to language, semantic processing, and reading, while the spatial context decision network was associated with navigation, episodic, and autobiographical memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by cognitive decoding analysis using Neurosynth, as shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The spatial context decision network was associated with navigation, episodic, and autobiographical memory.
source: Cognitive decoding of these connectivity maps using Neurosynth (Figure 3f) revealed that the semantic decision network was associated with terms related to language, semantic processing, and reading, while the spatial context decision network was associated with navigation, episodic, and autobiographical memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by cognitive decoding analysis using Neurosynth, as shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Semantic decision regions were more connected with lateral and ventral occipital cortex.
source: Semantic decision regions were more connected with lateral and ventral occipital cortex, whilst spatial context decision regions showed more connectivity with medial occipital, ventromedial temporal (including parahippocampal), and dorsal LOC.
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic connectivity analysis from Study 3, as shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Spatial context decision regions showed more connectivity with medial occipital, ventromedial temporal (including parahippocampal), and dorsal LOC.
source: Semantic decision regions were more connected with lateral and ventral occipital cortex, whilst spatial context decision regions showed more connectivity with medial occipital, ventromedial temporal (including parahippocampal), and dorsal LOC.
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic connectivity analysis from Study 3, as shown in Figure 3g.

claim: There was stronger connectivity between object probe regions and semantic versus spatial context decision regions.
source: Post hoc contrasts confirmed there was stronger connectivity between object probe regions and semantic versus spatial context decision regions (t(190)=3.98, p<0.001), and between scene probe regions and spatial context versus semantic decision regions (t(190)=20.07, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by seed-to-ROI connectivity analysis from Study 3 (t(190)=3.98, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There was stronger connectivity between scene probe regions and spatial context versus semantic decision regions.
source: Post hoc contrasts confirmed there was stronger connectivity between object probe regions and semantic versus spatial context decision regions (t(190)=3.98, p<0.001), and between scene probe regions and spatial context versus semantic decision regions (t(190)=20.07, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by seed-to-ROI connectivity analysis from Study 3 (t(190)=20.07, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There was stronger intrinsic connectivity between DMN regions implicated in semantic decisions and object probe regions.
source: The DMN-to-visual ANOVA confirmed this pattern: again, there was a main effect of ROI (F(1,190)=36.91, p<0.001) and a seed by ROI interaction (F(1,190)=218.42, p<0.001), with post hoc contrasts confirming stronger intrinsic connectivity between DMN regions implicated in semantic decisions and object probe regions (t(190)=11.63, p<0.001), and between DMN regions engaged by spatial context decisions and scene probe regions (t(190)=6.17, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by seed-to-ROI connectivity analysis from Study 3 (t(190)=11.63, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 4c.

claim: There was stronger intrinsic connectivity between DMN regions engaged by spatial context decisions and scene probe regions.
source: The DMN-to-visual ANOVA confirmed this pattern: again, there was a main effect of ROI (F(1,190)=36.91, p<0.001) and a seed by ROI interaction (F(1,190)=218.42, p<0.001), with post hoc contrasts confirming stronger intrinsic connectivity between DMN regions implicated in semantic decisions and object probe regions (t(190)=11.63, p<0.001), and between DMN regions engaged by spatial context decisions and scene probe regions (t(190)=6.17, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by seed-to-ROI connectivity analysis from Study 3 (t(190)=6.17, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The semantic pathway was predominantly characterised by FT-DMN and visual central regions in the Yeo et al., 2011, 17-network parcellation.
source: The semantic pathway was predominantly characterised by FT-DMN and visual central regions in the Yeo et al., 2011, 17-network parcellation, whilst the spatial context pathway reflected core and MT-DMN, and visual peripheral networks (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by network composition analysis, as shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The spatial context pathway reflected core and MT-DMN, and visual peripheral networks.
source: The semantic pathway was predominantly characterised by FT-DMN and visual central regions in the Yeo et al., 2011, 17-network parcellation, whilst the spatial context pathway reflected core and MT-DMN, and visual peripheral networks (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by network composition analysis, as shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Correlations between the semantic probe and decision phases' univariate activation and the semantic pathway were higher than non-pathway correlations.
source: Correlations between the semantic probe and decision phases' univariate activation and the semantic pathway were higher than non-pathway correlations and an equivalent pattern was seen for the spatial context pathway (Figure 4g; for exact t and p values associated with these comparisons see Supplementary file 2– Paired t-tests contrasting spatial similarity of participant-level activation with group-level context and semantic pathways and non-pathways), confirming that dissociable visual-to-DMN responses associated with semantic and spatial cognition are reliably present for individual participants.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis, as shown in Figure 4g.

claim: An equivalent pattern of higher pathway correlations was seen for the spatial context pathway.
source: Correlations between the semantic probe and decision phases' univariate activation and the semantic pathway were higher than non-pathway correlations and an equivalent pattern was seen for the spatial context pathway (Figure 4g; for exact t and p values associated with these comparisons see Supplementary file 2– Paired t-tests contrasting spatial similarity of participant-level activation with group-level context and semantic pathways and non-pathways), confirming that dissociable visual-to-DMN responses associated with semantic and spatial cognition are reliably present for individual participants.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis, as shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Object probe visual regions showed stronger structural connectivity to the semantic decision DMN regions.
source: Post hoc comparisons confirmed stronger structural connectivity from the semantic probe visual regions to the semantic decision DMN regions; likewise, the spatial context probe visual regions showed stronger structural connectivity to the spatial context decision DMN regions (semantic probe visual: t(163)=8.25, p<0.001; context probe visual: t(163)=478.66, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural connectivity analysis using HCP data (t(163)=8.25, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Spatial context probe visual regions showed stronger structural connectivity to the spatial context decision DMN regions.
source: Post hoc comparisons confirmed stronger structural connectivity from the semantic probe visual regions to the semantic decision DMN regions; likewise, the spatial context probe visual regions showed stronger structural connectivity to the spatial context decision DMN regions (semantic probe visual: t(163)=8.25, p<0.001; context probe visual: t(163)=478.66, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural connectivity analysis using HCP data (t(163)=478.66, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 4h.

claim: There were no differences between the two tasks during the probe phase in gradient space.
source: The results (Figure 5a) showed that there were no differences between the two tasks during the probe phase, while the decision phase was associated with task effects: DMN peaks for semantic decisions were more distant from sensory-motor cortex on the principal gradient, compared with spatial context decisions (t(1,26)=2.34, p=0.027), consistent with the view that semantic cognition draws on more abstract and heteromodal representations in DMN.
evidence: The claim is supported by gradient analysis, as shown in Figure 5a.

claim: DMN peaks for semantic decisions were more distant from sensory-motor cortex on the principal gradient, compared with spatial context decisions.
source: The results (Figure 5a) showed that there were no differences between the two tasks during the probe phase, while the decision phase was associated with task effects: DMN peaks for semantic decisions were more distant from sensory-motor cortex on the principal gradient, compared with spatial context decisions (t(1,26)=2.34, p=0.027), consistent with the view that semantic cognition draws on more abstract and heteromodal representations in DMN.
evidence: The claim is supported by gradient analysis (t(1,26)=2.34, p=0.027), as shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Responses for the spatial context task were closer to the visual end of the second gradient.
source: In addition, responses for the spatial context task were closer to the visual end of the second gradient, while responses for the semantic task were somewhat more balanced across visual and auditory-motor ends of this gradient (t(1,26)=3.31, p=0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by gradient analysis (t(1,26)=3.31, p=0.003), as shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Responses for the semantic task were somewhat more balanced across visual and auditory-motor ends of the second gradient.
source: In addition, responses for the spatial context task were closer to the visual end of the second gradient, while responses for the semantic task were somewhat more balanced across visual and auditory-motor ends of this gradient (t(1,26)=3.31, p=0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by gradient analysis (t(1,26)=3.31, p=0.003), as shown in Figure 5a.

claim: For scene probes in the spatial context task, the MCB>SCB contrast elicited a stronger response in dorsal LOC and retrosplenial cortex.
source: For scene probes in the spatial context task, the MCB>SCB contrast elicited a stronger response in dorsal LOC and retrosplenial cortex (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI analysis from Study 1, as shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The SCB>MCB contrast activated an adjacent region of right angular gyrus.
source: The SCB>MCB contrast activated an adjacent region of right angular gyrus (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI analysis from Study 1, as shown in Figure 6b.

claim: For semantic probes, the contrast of MCB>SCB identified greater engagement in distributed parietal, occipital, and temporal regions, associated with the multiple-demand network.
source: For semantic probes, the contrast of MCB>SCB identified greater engagement in distributed parietal, occipital, and temporal regions, associated with the multiple-demand network (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI analysis from Study 1, as shown in Figure 6c.

claim: There were no clusters that showed a stronger response to SCB than MCB probes for the semantic task.
source: There were no clusters that showed a stronger response to SCB than MCB probes for the semantic task.
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI analysis from Study 1.

claim: The context pathway was most connected to the spatial context MCB>SCB clusters.
source: Post hoc comparisons showed the context pathway was most connected to the spatial context MCB>SCB clusters, less connected to the spatial context SCB>MCB (when semantic information was also relevant to the response), and least connected to the semantic MCB>SCB regions (context MCB>context SCB: t(1,190)=34.91, p<0.001; context SCB>semantic MCB: t(1,190)=5.18, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by seed-to-ROI connectivity analysis from Study 3 (t(1,190)=34.91, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The semantic pathway was most connected to the semantic MCB>SCB regions.
source: The opposite pattern of connectivity was found for the semantic pathway, which was most connected to the semantic MCB>SCB regions, less connected to the spatial context SCB>MCB, and least connected to the spatial context MCB>SCB clusters (semantic MCB>context SCB: t(1,190)=16.93, p<0.001; context SCB>context MCB: t(1,190)=10.59, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by seed-to-ROI connectivity analysis from Study 3 (t(1,190)=16.93, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Spatial context SCB>MCB regions showed an intermediate pattern of connectivity to both pathways.
source: In this way, spatial context SCB>MCB regions, which reflected the engagement of semantic information in a spatial context task, showed an intermediate pattern of connectivity to both pathways.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connectivity analysis results showing intermediate connectivity values, as shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Functional subdivisions of visual cortex and DMN sit at opposing ends of parallel streams of information processing that support visually mediated semantic and spatial cognition.
source: We show that functional subdivisions of visual cortex and DMN sit at opposing ends of parallel streams of information processing that support visually mediated semantic and spatial cognition, providing convergent evidence from univariate and multivariate task responses, intrinsic functional and structural connectivity.
evidence: The claim is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple types of evidence (univariate, multivariate, functional connectivity, structural connectivity) presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A lateral ventral occipital to fronto-temporal DMN pathway was primarily engaged by semantic judgements.
source: A lateral ventral occipital to fronto-temporal DMN pathway was primarily engaged by semantic judgements, while a medial visual to medial temporal DMN pathway supported spatial context judgements.
evidence: The claim is a main finding of the study, supported by task activation, connectivity, and structural data presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: A medial visual to medial temporal DMN pathway supported spatial context judgements.
source: A lateral ventral occipital to fronto-temporal DMN pathway was primarily engaged by semantic judgements, while a medial visual to medial temporal DMN pathway supported spatial context judgements.
evidence: The claim is a main finding of the study, supported by task activation, connectivity, and structural data presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: The semantic pathway was both further from unimodal systems and more balanced between visual and auditory-motor regions compared with the spatial pathway.
source: These pathways had distinctive locations in functional connectivity space: the semantic pathway was both further from unimodal systems and more balanced between visual and auditory-motor regions compared with the spatial pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by gradient analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: When semantic and spatial context information could be integrated (in buildings containing objects from a single category), regions at the intersection of these pathways responded.
source: When semantic and spatial context information could be integrated (in buildings containing objects from a single category), regions at the intersection of these pathways responded, suggesting that parallel processing streams interact at multiple levels of the cortical hierarchy to produce coherent memory-guided cognition.
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate and multivariate analyses of SCB vs MCB conditions presented in Figure 6.

claim: Parallel processing streams interact at multiple levels of the cortical hierarchy to produce coherent memory-guided cognition.
source: When semantic and spatial context information could be integrated (in buildings containing objects from a single category), regions at the intersection of these pathways responded, suggesting that parallel processing streams interact at multiple levels of the cortical hierarchy to produce coherent memory-guided cognition.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings regarding integration regions, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The distinction between FT-DMN and MT-DMN subsystems is not organized according to visual coupling.
source: Our findings also suggest that the distinction between these subsystems is not organised according to visual coupling; instead, DMN organisation arises from differential connectivity between distinct visual and DMN regions that gives rise to partially segregated pathways that process information about locations and meanings.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings, based on the observed differential connectivity patterns.

claim: DMN organisation arises from differential connectivity between distinct visual and DMN regions that gives rise to partially segregated pathways that process information about locations and meanings.
source: Our findings also suggest that the distinction between these subsystems is not organised according to visual coupling; instead, DMN organisation arises from differential connectivity between distinct visual and DMN regions that gives rise to partially segregated pathways that process information about locations and meanings.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings, based on the observed differential connectivity patterns.

claim: Visual responses to scenes and objects reflect entry points to semantic and spatial processing pathways.
source: Visual responses to scenes and objects reflect entry points to these processing pathways such that the key distinction between FT-DMN and MT-DMN relates to the type of information being processed, as opposed to how the information is accessed.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings regarding the organization of visual-to-DMN pathways.

claim: The key distinction between FT-DMN and MT-DMN relates to the type of information being processed, as opposed to how the information is accessed.
source: Visual responses to scenes and objects reflect entry points to these processing pathways such that the key distinction between FT-DMN and MT-DMN relates to the type of information being processed, as opposed to how the information is accessed.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings regarding the organization of DMN subsystems.

claim: There is a domain-specific organization for working memory in prefrontal cortex with dorsal and ventral streams associated with the maintenance of item location and identity respectively.
source: Our observed dissociation between semantic and spatial context pathways echoes a similar domain-specific organisation for working memory in prefrontal cortex (Levy and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Romanski, 2004), in which there are dorsal and ventral streams associated with the maintenance of item location and identity respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Levy and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Romanski, 2004).

claim: Deen and Freiwald, 2021, found a similar dissociation between places and people in the DMN and other areas of association cortex.
source: Deen and Freiwald, 2021, found a similar dissociation between places and people (instead of objects) in the DMN and other areas of association cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Deen and Freiwald, 2021.

claim: The FT subsystem is thought to rely on the abstraction of information from sensory-motor inputs.
source: The FT subsystem is thought to rely on the abstraction of information from sensory-motor inputs (; Smallwood et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Smallwood et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The MT subsystem uses a relational code that can capture spatial relations to successfully navigate complex environments.
source: The MT subsystem, on the other hand, uses a relational code that can capture spatial relations to successfully navigate complex environments (Eichenbaum, 2004; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014; Zeidman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Eichenbaum, 2004; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014; Zeidman et al., 2015).

claim: Spatial location is more dependent on peripheral vision, while object recognition is dependent on central fixation.
source: One possibility is that, at the visual end of these pathways, spatial location is more dependent on peripheral vision, while object recognition is dependent on central fixation (Hasson et al., 2002; Levy et al., 2001); consequently, the distinct visual-to-DMN pathways we have recovered may reflect a basic property of how peripheral and central visual regions project to DMN.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Hasson et al., 2002; Levy et al., 2001) and represents a possible explanation for the observed pathways.

claim: The distinct visual-to-DMN pathways may reflect a basic property of how peripheral and central visual regions project to DMN.
source: One possibility is that, at the visual end of these pathways, spatial location is more dependent on peripheral vision, while object recognition is dependent on central fixation (Hasson et al., 2002; Levy et al., 2001); consequently, the distinct visual-to-DMN pathways we have recovered may reflect a basic property of how peripheral and central visual regions project to DMN.
evidence: The claim is indicated by 'may reflect' and represents a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Right angular gyrus is implicated in the integration of information from multiple domains into a rich, meaningful context that can guide ongoing cognition.
source: The response we identified in right angular gyrus when object semantic and spatial context information was aligned is consistent with earlier studies implicating this brain region in the integration of information from multiple domains into a rich, meaningful context that can guide ongoing cognition (Lanzoni et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lanzoni et al., 2020.

claim: Neurons in angular gyrus represent high-dimensional inputs on a low-dimensional manifold encoding the relative position of items in physical space and abstract conceptual space.
source: One recent proposal suggests that neurons in this area represent high-dimensional inputs on a low-dimensional manifold encoding the relative position of items in physical space and abstract conceptual space (Summerfield et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Summerfield et al., 2020 and represents a theoretical proposal.

claim: Angular gyrus might have the capacity to form representations that are not dominated by one type of input or code.
source: This region, which is maximally distant from sensory-motor cortex and equidistant from visual and motor cortex, might have the capacity to form representations that are not dominated by one type of input or code.
evidence: The claim is indicated by 'might' and represents a speculative interpretation based on the region's position in connectivity space.

claim: Previous research has established a key role of the AG in context integration.
source: Previous research has established a key role of the AG in context integration (Bonnici et al., 2016; Branzi et al., 2020; Ramanan et al., 2018) and specifically, in guiding multimodal decisions and behaviour (Humphreys et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2017; Yazar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Bonnici et al., 2016; Branzi et al., 2020; Ramanan et al., 2018; Humphreys et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2017; Yazar et al., 2017).

claim: Some recent proposals suggest a causal role of right AG in the early establishment of meaningful contexts, allowing semantic integration across modalities.
source: Although some recent proposals suggest a causal role of right AG in the early establishment of meaningful contexts, allowing semantic integration across modalities (Bocca et al., 2015; Muggleton et al., 2008; Olk et al., 2015; Petitet et al., 2015; Seghier, 2023), the majority of this research points to left, rather than right, AG as a key region for integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Bocca et al., 2015; Muggleton et al., 2008; Olk et al., 2015; Petitet et al., 2015; Seghier, 2023).

claim: Visuospatial memory processes might be somewhat right lateralised.
source: We might have observed involvement of the right AG in our study since people were integrating semantic and spatial information, and visuospatial memory processes might be somewhat right lateralised (cf. Sormaz et al., 2017) and more strongly connected to right than left AG.
evidence: The claim is indicated by 'might be' and is supported by citation to Sormaz et al., 2017.

claim: Topography is highly relevant to information integration since adjacent brain regions tend to share a high degree of functional connectivity and represent similar information.
source: These different levels of integration shared a common characteristic: in both cases, the region implicated in integration was spatially interposed between the pathways, consistent with the view that topography is highly relevant to information integration since adjacent brain regions tend to share a high degree of functional connectivity and represent similar information.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the observed spatial relationships between integration regions and pathways, drawing on established principles of brain organization.

claim: Common visual-to-DMN pathways might support memory access from vision and subserve the generation of visual features when imagining objects versus scenes.
source: While we might assume that common visual-to-DMN pathways support memory access from vision (as in this study), and subserve the generation of visual features when imagining objects versus scenes, this hypothesis awaits empirical investigation.
evidence: The claim is indicated by 'might assume' and 'awaits empirical investigation', representing a speculative hypothesis for future research.

claim: It remains unclear if there are analogous pathways from auditory or somatomotor cortex to DMN.
source: Moreover, our pathways are vision-specific, and it remains unclear if there are analogous pathways from auditory or somatomotor cortex to DMN.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the current study and identifies an area for future research.

claim: The generality of these pathways must be confirmed across tasks.
source: The generality of these pathways must be confirmed across tasks, since spatial representations are likely to interact with other representational codes, including emotion and social information – the interdigitated pathways highlighted in these circumstances (Braga and Buckner, 2017; DiNicola et al., 2020) might show anatomical differences or be broadly the same as the pathways uncovered here.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation and identifies future research directions, with citations (Braga and Buckner, 2017; DiNicola et al., 2020).

claim: Some researchers have argued for a 'third pathway' for aspects of social visual cognition.
source: On the other hand, some researchers have argued for a 'third pathway' for aspects of social visual cognition (Pitcher, 2023; Pitcher and Ungerleider, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Pitcher, 2023; Pitcher and Ungerleider, 2021).

claim: The dissociations found in task responses, intrinsic functional connectivity, and white matter connections support the view that there are at least two distinct routes between visual and heteromodal DMN regions.
source: The dissociations we found in task responses, intrinsic functional connectivity, and white matter connections all support the view that there are at least two distinct routes between visual and heteromodal DMN regions, yet this does not necessarily imply that there is a continuous sequence of cortical areas that extend from visual cortex to DMN – and given our findings of structural connectivity differences that relate to the functional subdivisions we observe, this is unlikely to be the sole mechanism underpinning our findings.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings, acknowledging both the evidence for distinct pathways and the complexity of their organization.

claim: A continuous sequence of cortical areas extending from visual cortex to DMN is unlikely to be the sole mechanism underpinning the observed pathways.
source: The dissociations we found in task responses, intrinsic functional connectivity, and white matter connections all support the view that there are at least two distinct routes between visual and heteromodal DMN regions, yet this does not necessarily imply that there is a continuous sequence of cortical areas that extend from visual cortex to DMN – and given our findings of structural connectivity differences that relate to the functional subdivisions we observe, this is unlikely to be the sole mechanism underpinning our findings.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the structural connectivity findings.
